frontmatter.title: GluonTS API Tutorial: Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting

children.value: This hands-on tutorial teaches you how to build probabilistic time series forecasts with
, an open-source Python library from AWS. You’ll go from raw data to evaluated predictions — learning the
Familiarity with machine learning concepts (training, testing, epochs)
No prior time series experience needed — we’ll explain everything as we go
How to prepare time series data for GluonTS (
How to configure, train, and evaluate three different forecasting models
When to pick each model for your problem
Direct mapping from recent history to future
Learns the data distribution without assumptions
We start with synthetic time series instead of real-world data. This lets you focus on
without getting distracted by domain complexity (missing values, reporting artifacts, policy effects, etc.).
We’ll progress through three levels of difficulty:
Can the model learn a clean periodic signal?
Can it handle trend + seasonality + weekly cycles + noise?
Can it adapt when the data’s behavior changes midway?
Once you’re comfortable with the mechanics here, move to
to see these models applied to real COVID-19 data.

import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

# Core GluonTS components for the API tutorial
from gluonts.torch.model.deepar import DeepAREstimator
from gluonts.torch.model.simple_feedforward import SimpleFeedForwardEstimator
from gluonts.torch.model.deep_npts import DeepNPTSEstimator
from gluonts.evaluation import make_evaluation_predictions

# All our utilities are in one place - much cleaner!
import GluonTS_utils as gluonts

print("Setup complete. Ready to explore GluonTS.")

children.value: Every GluonTS model follows the same five steps. We’ll walk through each one in detail as we go, but here’s the big picture:

Step 1  Prepare data      →  ListDataset({"start", "target"}, freq)
Step 2  Configure model    →  SomeEstimator(prediction_length, context_length, ...)
Step 3  Train              →  predictor = estimator.train(train_ds)
Step 4  Generate forecasts →  make_evaluation_predictions(test_ds, predictor, num_samples)
Step 5  Evaluate           →  forecast.mean, forecast.quantile(q), forecast.samples
Let’s see this in action, starting with the simplest possible time series.
We begin with a pure sine wave plus a small amount of Gaussian noise. This is the easiest pattern a model can encounter: perfectly periodic, no trend, no regime changes.
If a model can’t forecast a sinusoid, something is fundamentally wrong. This gives us a clean baseline to verify our pipeline works before increasing complexity.

sin_df = gluonts.generate_sinusoid(
    n_points=365,
    period=30,
    amplitude=10.0,
    noise_std=1.0,
    seed=42,
)

gluonts.plot_synthetic_series(sin_df, title="Sinusoid: 30-day cycle, low noise")
Before any model can train, your data must be in GluonTS’s
format. Each entry is a dictionary with:
— a 1-D array of the values you want to forecast

utility handles the train/test split and conversion for you. The last
— we’ll cover that in the example notebook with real COVID-19 covariates. For now, we’re keeping it simple: just a target series.

sin_data = gluonts.prepare_synthetic_dataset(
    sin_df,
    prediction_length=PREDICTION_LENGTH,

gluonts.plot_train_test_split(sin_data, title="Sinusoid - Train / Test Split")

children.value: We use three standard metrics to measure forecast quality:
(Mean Absolute Error) — average absolute difference, in original units. Easy to interpret.
(Root Mean Square Error) — like MAE, but penalizes large errors more heavily.
(Mean Absolute Percentage Error) — percentage error, so you can compare across different scales.

sin_actuals = sin_data["test_df"]["value"].values
deepar_sin_metrics = gluonts.calculate_metrics(deepar_forecast.mean, sin_actuals)

gluonts.print_metrics(deepar_sin_metrics, model_name="DeepAR on Sinusoid")

children.value: Level 3: Regime Change — The Hard Problem

children.label: Level 3: Regime Change — The Hard Problem

children.value: This is where things get interesting. The series behaves one way for the first half, then
to a different baseline, amplitude, and frequency.
A new COVID variant causing a sudden surge
A product going viral and changing demand patterns
A policy change shifting economic indicators
Most models struggle here because their training data comes from the old regime, but they need to forecast in the new one.

regime_df = gluonts.generate_regime_change(
    n_points=365,
    changepoint_frac=0.6,
    noise_std=1.5,
    seed=42,
)

gluonts.plot_synthetic_series(
    regime_df, title="Regime Change: behavior shifts at day ~219"
)

regime_data = gluonts.prepare_synthetic_dataset(
    regime_df,
    prediction_length=PREDICTION_LENGTH,
)

gluonts.plot_train_test_split(
    regime_data, title="Regime Change - Train / Test Split"
)

Let’s run DeepAR on the same regime-change data to see how it compares. Because DeepAR assumes a parametric distribution learned from the full training set, it may struggle with the post-shift behavior.

    prediction_length=PREDICTION_LENGTH,
    context_length=60,
    freq="D",
    num_layers=2,
    hidden_size=40,
    trainer_kwargs={"max_epochs": 5},
)

deepar_regime_pred = deepar_regime_est.train(regime_data["train_ds"])

forecast_it, ts_it = make_evaluation_predictions(
    dataset=regime_data["test_ds"],
    predictor=deepar_regime_pred,
    num_samples=100,
)
deepar_regime_fc = list(forecast_it)[0]

gluonts.plot_forecast_result(regime_data, deepar_regime_fc, model_name="DeepAR")
